sections.title: Kinematic Equations for Motion in a Straight Line with Constant Acceleration

slides.title: What the Position-Time Graph Shows
slides.kicker: Every journey leaves a trail on paper
bullets: A position-time graph represents the motion of an object, that is, how its position changes with time.
Time is marked along the X-axis and position along the Y-axis, so each point shows where the object was at that instant.
From such a graph you can read the position of the object at each instant of time.
slides.note: Graph padh ke poora safar dikh jaata hai.

slides.title: Straight Line, Constant Velocity
slides.kicker: Equal 20 m steps, every single time
bullets: In Fig. 4.13a, the object covers equal displacements of 20 m in equal intervals of time.
Equal displacement in equal time means the magnitude of velocity is constant.
So a straight-line position-time graph indicates that the object is moving with a constant velocity.
slides.note: Straight graph means steady velocity. Seedha raasta!

slides.title: Curved Graph Means Accelerated Motion
slides.kicker: When the line bends, motion speeds up
bullets: In Fig. 4.13b, the magnitudes of displacement grow larger in equal intervals of time, so the magnitude of velocity is increasing.
A curved position-time graph indicates the velocity is not constant.
Velocity that keeps changing means the object is in accelerated motion.

slides.title: Build the Slope Triangle
slides.kicker: Activity 4.4 draws a helpful triangle
bullets: Take a part AB of the plotted position-time graph, as done in Activity 4.4.
From point A draw a line parallel to the X-axis, and from point B draw a line parallel to the Y-axis.
The two lines form triangle ABC, where BC represents the change in position (s2 - s1) and CA represents the change in time (t2 - t1).

items: Pick two points A and B on the graph
From A, draw a line parallel to the X-axis
From B, draw a line parallel to the Y-axis
Triangle ABC forms: BC is change in position, CA is change in time

slides.title: Slope Gives Average Velocity
slides.kicker: Rise over run, graph style
bullets: Divide the change in position BC by the change in time CA to get the average velocity, exactly as in Eq. (4.2a).
Geometrically, this ratio (s2 - s1)/(t2 - t1) is called the slope of the line AB joining the initial position A and the final position B.
So from a position-time graph, positions at two instants are enough to calculate the average velocity.
slides.note: BC divided by CA — graph se velocity nikal gayi.

slides.title: Reading a Position-Time Graph
slides.kicker: Two readings, one full story
bullets: A position-time graph hands you two gifts: the position at any instant and the average velocity between two instants.
A straight line section means constant velocity; a curved section means accelerated motion.
The steeper the line, the larger the magnitude of the velocity it shows.

slides.title: Velocity-Time Graph Basics
slides.kicker: Now velocity gets its own graph
bullets: A velocity-time graph represents the change in velocity of an object with time.
You can plot it in a manner similar to the position-time graph, following the steps of Activity 4.3.
Each point on the graph gives the magnitude of velocity of the object at that instant.

items: Time on X-axis, velocity on Y-axis

slides.title: Steady 72 km/h Highway Drive
slides.kicker: Flat line, zero acceleration, smooth cruise
bullets: A car moves in the same direction on a straight stretch of highway at a steady velocity of 72 km/h, which is 20 m/s.
Its velocity-time graph is a straight line parallel to the X-axis, as in Fig. 4.17a.
The height of this line never changes, so the velocity is constant and the acceleration is zero.
slides.note: 72 km/h means 20 m/s. Dono ek hi baat.

slides.title: Speeding Up at Constant Acceleration
slides.kicker: Equal jumps in velocity every second
bullets: Another car starts moving from rest, and its velocity increases with time as listed in Table 4.5.
In equal intervals of time the velocity increases by equal amounts, so the acceleration is constant.
Its velocity-time graph (Fig. 4.17b) is a straight line sloping upward: velocity increasing with constant acceleration in the direction of velocity.

items: Velocity rises by equal amounts in equal times

slides.title: Slowing Down at Constant Acceleration
slides.kicker: Braking gently, equal drops each second
bullets: A third car moves with a velocity of 15.0 m/s, and its velocity decreases with time as listed in Table 4.6.
In equal intervals of time the velocity decreases by equal amounts, so this too is constant acceleration.
Its velocity-time graph (Fig. 4.17c) is a straight line sloping downward: the acceleration acts opposite to the direction of velocity.

slides.title: Slope Gives Acceleration
slides.kicker: Steeper line, harder acceleration
bullets: The slope of the line on a velocity-time graph tells how fast the velocity is changing with time, that is, the acceleration.
For the steady 20 m/s car in Fig. 4.17a, there is no change in the height of the line from the X-axis, so the slope is zero.
Zero slope means constant velocity and zero acceleration; rising or falling slopes mean velocity changing at a constant rate.

items: Pick two points on the v-t line
Find the change in velocity between them
Find the change in time between them
Divide change in velocity by change in time to get acceleration

slides.note: Yahan slope acceleration deta hai, velocity nahi. Dhyan se!

slides.title: Area Under the Graph
slides.kicker: Area under the line hides displacement
bullets: Besides velocity at each instant and acceleration from the slope, a velocity-time graph hides one more treasure.
The displacement of the object during a time interval is given by the area enclosed under its velocity-time graph.
For a straight-line graph this area can be split into simple shapes, like the rectangle OACD plus the triangle ABC used for region OABD.

slides.title: Constant Acceleration, Special Case
slides.kicker: When a never changes, equations appear
bullets: Let us consider the special case of motion with constant acceleration and derive equations to analyse such motion.
Since the acceleration is constant, the acceleration at each instant equals the average acceleration over any time interval.
This single fact lets us turn the definition of acceleration into equations that predict motion.

slides.title: First Kinematic Equation
slides.kicker: Slope trick turns into an equation
bullets: Using the definition of average acceleration (Eq. 4.3c), a = (v - u)/t, where u is the initial velocity at t = 0 and v is the final velocity at time t.
Multiply both sides by t to get at = v - u, then rearrange.
This gives v = u + at (Eq. 4.4a), which calculates the velocity at all times when u and a are known.

items: Multiply both sides by t: at = v - u

slides.title: Displacement as Graph Area
slides.kicker: Rectangle plus triangle equals displacement
bullets: The displacement s during time t equals the area enclosed within OABD on the velocity-time graph of Eq. 4.4a (Fig. 4.19).
Split OABD into the rectangle OACD with area AO × DO, that is u × t, and the triangle ABC.
Triangle ABC has base CA = t and height BC = v - u, so its area is (1/2) × t × (v - u).

slides.title: Second Kinematic Equation
slides.kicker: Swap v minus u for at
bullets: Adding the two areas gives s = u × t + (1/2) × t × (v - u).
Substitute the value of (v - u) from Eq. 4.4a, where v - u = at.
The result is s = ut + (1/2)at^2 (Eq. 4.4b), the displacement equation for constant acceleration.

items: Start with s = ut + (1/2) × t × (v - u)
Use v - u = at from Eq. 4.4a

slides.note: Half a t squared yaad rakho, exam favourite.

slides.title: Third Kinematic Equation
slides.kicker: Kick time out, keep the rest
bullets: Combining the primary equations in different ways gives three more equations; here we eliminate t from Eq. 4.4b.
From Eq. 4.4a we get t = (v - u)/a, and we substitute this into Eq. 4.4b.
Expanding and simplifying leaves v^2 = u^2 + 2as (Eq. 4.4c), an equation with no time in it.

slides.title: Five Quantities, Three Equations
slides.kicker: Five quantities, three tidy equations
bullets: For motion in a straight line with constant acceleration, five quantities matter: displacement s, time interval t, initial velocity u, final velocity v and acceleration a.
Eq. 4.4a, Eq. 4.4b and Eq. 4.4c, known as the kinematic equations, link all five of them.
These equations give a mathematical description of how the motion of an object changes with time; two more equations wait in The Journey Beyond at the chapter's end.

slides.title: Distance Versus Displacement on Circles
slides.kicker: Curve ABC versus straight line AC
bullets: When an object moves in a circular path, its motion is called circular motion.
A child on a moving merry-go-round travels from A to B to C: the distance travelled is the curve ABC, while the displacement is the straight line AC.
As you can see, the two are not equal, even for the same ride.

left.title: Distance travelled
items: always grows as the child moves

right.title: Displacement
items: the shortest route from start to finish
depends only on start and end points

slides.title: One Full Revolution
slides.kicker: Round and round, back to start
bullets: The distance travelled by the child in making one revolution equals the circumference of the circle.
If the radius of the circular path is R, the distance for one revolution is 2πR.
The displacement after one revolution is zero, since the child comes back to the original position.
slides.note: Full circle, zero displacement. Baaki sab distance.

slides.title: Speed of a Revolution
slides.kicker: Circumference divided by time T
bullets: If the object takes time T to make one revolution, its average speed follows from Eq. 4.1.
The average speed is v_av = 2πR/T (Eq. 4.5), the circumference divided by the time of one round.
The average velocity during the same interval T is 0, because the displacement is 0.

slides.title: Uniform Circular Motion Defined
slides.kicker: Speed steady, direction dancing
bullets: Uniform circular motion is the motion of an object moving in a circular path with constant, that is uniform, speed.
The speed stays constant, but the direction of velocity at an instant does not: it keeps changing.
Because the direction of velocity changes continuously, uniform circular motion is accelerated motion.

slides.title: From Rectangle to Circle
slides.kicker: An athlete's track becomes a circle
bullets: An athlete running at uniform speed on a rectangular track ABCD changes direction four times to complete one round.
On a hexagonal track the athlete changes direction six times per round (Fig. 4.23).
If the number of sides increases indefinitely, turns come more and more frequently, and the track approaches a circle where the direction of velocity changes continuously.

slides.title: Marble in a Ring
slides.kicker: Activity 4.5 spins a marble
bullets: Take a ring, such as an adhesive tape ring, and one marble for Activity 4.5.
Place the ring flat on a smooth surface and throw the marble inside it.
The marble rotates along the inner boundary of the ring, circling with its direction of motion changing at every point.

items: Take an adhesive tape ring and a marble
Place the ring flat on a smooth surface
Throw the marble inside the ring
Watch it rotate along the inner boundary

flashcards.front: What does a straight-line position-time graph tell you about the motion?
flashcards.back: The object is moving with a constant velocity, since equal displacements happen in equal intervals of time.

flashcards.front: What does a curved position-time graph indicate?
flashcards.back: The velocity is not constant, so the object is in accelerated motion.

flashcards.front: How do you find average velocity from a position-time graph?
flashcards.back: Read positions s1 and s2 at instants t1 and t2, then compute (s2 - s1)/(t2 - t1), which is the slope of line AB.

flashcards.front: In the slope triangle ABC on a position-time graph, what do sides BC and CA represent?
flashcards.back: BC represents the change in position (s2 - s1) and CA represents the change in time (t2 - t1).

flashcards.front: A car moves at a steady 72 km/h. What does its velocity-time graph look like?
flashcards.back: A straight line parallel to the X-axis at 20 m/s, and its acceleration is zero.

flashcards.front: What does the slope of a line on a velocity-time graph give?
flashcards.back: The acceleration, that is, how fast the velocity is changing with time.

flashcards.front: A velocity-time line rises by equal amounts in equal times. What motion is this?
flashcards.back: Velocity increasing with constant acceleration, in the direction of the velocity.

flashcards.front: What does the area enclosed under a velocity-time graph give?
flashcards.back: The displacement of the object during that time interval.

flashcards.front: Write the kinematic equation that gives final velocity with constant acceleration.
flashcards.back: v = u + at, where u is initial velocity, a is acceleration and t is the time interval (Eq. 4.4a).

flashcards.front: Write the kinematic equation for displacement with constant acceleration.
flashcards.back: s = ut + (1/2)at^2, derived from the area of the v-t graph (Eq. 4.4b).

flashcards.front: Which kinematic equation links v, u, a and s without time?
Why can we use average acceleration at every instant when acceleration is constant?
flashcards.back: Because constant acceleration is the same at each instant, it equals the average acceleration over any time interval.
The motion of an object moving in a circular path with constant (uniform) speed.

flashcards.front: After one revolution of a circle of radius R, what are the distance and displacement?
flashcards.back: Distance equals the circumference 2πR, while displacement is zero because the object returns to its starting position.

flashcards.front: What is the average speed for one revolution that takes time T?
flashcards.back: v_av = 2πR/T (Eq. 4.5); the average velocity over the same interval is 0 since displacement is 0.

flashcards.front: In uniform circular motion, what keeps changing even though speed is constant?
flashcards.back: The direction of velocity changes continuously as the object moves along the circular path.

quiz.q: The position-time graph of an object is a straight line. What does this indicate?
options: The object is at rest throughout
The object moves with constant velocity
The object is in accelerated motion
The velocity of the object is zero
quiz.why: Fig. 4.13a shows a straight line position-time graph means the object moves with constant velocity.

quiz.q: In Fig. 4.13a the object covers equal displacements of 20 m in equal intervals of time. Its velocity magnitude is:
quiz.why: Equal displacements of 20 m in equal time intervals mean the magnitude of velocity is constant.

quiz.q: On a position-time graph you form triangle ABC, where BC is change in position and CA is change in time. What is BC divided by CA?
quiz.why: By Eq. (4.2a), dividing change in position by change in time gives the average velocity, the slope of line AB.

quiz.q: A position-time graph is curved, rising more and more steeply as time passes. What is happening to the motion?
options: Velocity is increasing, so the motion is accelerated
Velocity is constant but displacement grows
The object pauses at each plotted point
quiz.why: Displacements grow in equal intervals, so velocity increases; a curved position-time graph means accelerated motion.

quiz.q: The book's car cruises a straight highway at 72 km/h. What is this velocity in m/s?
A velocity-time graph is a straight line parallel to the X-axis. What is the acceleration?
quiz.why: For Fig. 4.17a there is no change in the height of the line, so the slope is zero and acceleration is zero.

quiz.q: A car starts from rest and its velocity increases by equal amounts in equal intervals (Table 4.5). Its velocity-time graph is:
options: A straight line sloping upward with constant acceleration
A horizontal line parallel to the X-axis
A curve that keeps getting flatter
A vertical straight line at t = 0
quiz.why: Fig. 4.17b shows velocity increasing with constant acceleration is a straight-line velocity-time graph.

quiz.q: A car moving at 15.0 m/s slows down, its velocity decreasing by equal amounts in equal times (Table 4.6). The acceleration is directed:
options: Opposite to the direction of velocity
quiz.why: Fig. 4.17c shows velocity decreasing with constant acceleration opposite to the direction of velocity.

quiz.q: Which of these is the first kinematic equation for motion with constant acceleration?
quiz.why: Eq. 4.4a, v = u + at, comes from the definition of average acceleration and gives velocity at all times.

quiz.q: In deriving s = ut + (1/2)at^2, the area OABD of the velocity-time graph is split into which two parts?
options: A rectangle of area (1/2)ut and a triangle of area (1/2)vt
Two triangles of equal area ut
A square of area u × t and a circle of area 2πR
A rectangle of area u × t plus a triangle of area (1/2) × t × (v - u)
quiz.why: Area OABD equals rectangle OACD with area u × t plus triangle ABC with area (1/2) × t × (v - u).

quiz.q: You know u, v, a and s but not the time. Which kinematic equation should you use?
quiz.why: Eq. 4.4c, v^2 = u^2 + 2as, was obtained by eliminating t, so it contains no time.

quiz.q: How exactly is the third kinematic equation derived from the two primary equations?
options: Displacement s is eliminated using s = ut
Time t is eliminated by substituting t = (v - u)/a into Eq. 4.4b
Acceleration a is eliminated using a = (v - u)/t
Initial velocity u is simply set to zero
quiz.why: The book eliminates t by substituting t = (v - u)/a from Eq. 4.4a into Eq. 4.4b, giving v^2 = u^2 + 2as.

quiz.q: An object moves in a circular path with constant speed. This particular motion is called:
quiz.why: Motion in a circular path with constant (uniform) speed is defined as uniform circular motion.

quiz.q: A child on a merry-go-round of radius R completes exactly one revolution. The displacement is:
quiz.why: After one revolution the child is back at the original position, so displacement is zero.

quiz.q: One revolution of radius R takes time T. What is the average velocity for that revolution?
quiz.why: Average velocity is displacement over time, and displacement for one full revolution is zero.

quiz.q: An athlete runs uniform-speed rounds on a rectangular track, then a hexagonal track, then a circular one (Fig. 4.23). The key change is:
options: Direction never changes, only speed changes
Direction changes 4 times, then 6 times, then continuously on the circle
Speed keeps increasing from track to track
Displacement after one round becomes larger
quiz.why: Fig. 4.23 shows 4 turns on the rectangle, 6 on the hexagon, and continuous direction change on the circle.

examples.title: Average Velocity from a Graph
examples.problem: A car moves along a straight road and its position-time graph is a straight line like Fig. 4.13a. From the graph, the position is 20 m at 2 s and 60 m at 6 s. Using the method of Activity 4.4, find the average velocity between these two instants.
steps: Read the two positions from the graph: s1 = 20 m at t1 = 2 s and s2 = 60 m at t2 = 6 s.
Form the slope triangle ABC: side BC is the change in position, s2 - s1 = 60 - 20 = 40 m, and side CA is the change in time, t2 - t1 = 6 - 2 = 4 s.
Divide change in position by change in time as in Eq. (4.2a): average velocity = BC/CA = 40/4.
Sanity check: the graph is a straight line, so equal 20 m displacements occur in equal 2 s intervals, matching a constant slope.
examples.answer: Average velocity = 10 m/s, which is the slope of the straight line AB on the position-time graph.

examples.title: Car Starting from Rest
examples.problem: A car starts from rest and moves in a straight line with a constant acceleration of 2 m/s^2 for 5 s. Using the kinematic equations, find its velocity at the end of 5 s and its displacement in that time, then verify with the third equation.
steps: Starting from rest means initial velocity u = 0. Given a = 2 m/s^2 and t = 5 s.
Velocity from Eq. 4.4a: v = u + at = 0 + 2 × 5 = 10 m/s.
Displacement from Eq. 4.4b: s = ut + (1/2)at^2 = 0 × 5 + (1/2) × 2 × 5^2 = 25 m.
Verify with Eq. 4.4c: v^2 = u^2 + 2as = 0 + 2 × 2 × 25 = 100, so v = 10 m/s, which matches the value from Eq. 4.4a.
examples.answer: Final velocity is 10 m/s and displacement is 25 m; all three kinematic equations agree.

examples.title: One Round on a Merry-Go-Round
examples.problem: A child rides a merry-go-round of radius 7 m and completes one revolution in 4 s. Taking π as 22/7, find the distance travelled, the displacement, the average speed and the average velocity for that one round.
steps: Distance in one revolution equals the circumference of the circle: 2πR = 2 × (22/7) × 7 = 44 m.
After one revolution the child is back at the original position, so the displacement is 0.
Average speed from Eq. 4.5: v_av = 2πR/T = 44/4 = 11 m/s.
Average velocity over the interval T is displacement divided by time, and since the displacement is 0, the average velocity is 0.
examples.answer: Distance 44 m, displacement 0, average speed 11 m/s and average velocity 0 for the single revolution.
